passage: Varun stared at the email from the school group: they had gone with the other company. Nitin's team, the one Varun had privately called "the flashy ones," had won it. His first reaction was a hot, tight feeling in his chest. He closed the laptop, walked to the stairwell of the office in Pune and came back with a different question. Could he ask the school group why? He called and asked politely. The answer surprised him: Nitin's team had run the demo on the school group's own sample data and replied to every question the same day. Varun pulled the team together that afternoon. "Next demo, we use their data. And nobody leaves a question overnight." At the industry meet the next month, he walked over and congratulated Nitin.

qa.q: What did the school group say Nitin's team did differently in the demo?
qa.a: Nitin's team ran the demo on the school group's own sample data and answered every question the same day.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when the email arrived, and what did he do with it?
qa.a: He felt a hot, tight sting in his chest, then steadied himself and turned it into curiosity, calling the client to ask why they had chosen the other company.

qa.q: What did Varun change after learning why he lost?
qa.a: He decided future demos would use the client's own data and that no question would wait overnight. 👍

qa.q: How might Nitin see Varun's congratulations at the meet?
qa.a: Nitin may be a little surprised and see it as a sign of respect from a rival, though Nitin might still stay watchful.

grounding: Shows a salesperson studying why a rival won a deal, improving his own offering and treating the competitor as a teacher.
